archetype: BG -1/-1 counter aristocrats on the combo axis: a converter engine whose median game mints bodies out of other cards' counters and turns those bodies into cards and drain, with one verified two-card kill and a mostly unresolved combo ceiling above it

role_assignment.default_role: Control/engine seat by default. You own a medium-to-long game: a repeatable -1/-1 source feeding a table-wide drain converter is 'an engine that scales', which strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock names as a source of inevitability, and 1/1 deathtouch Snakes make your early turns cheap to survive. Do not try to be the beatdown with combat — Hapatra is a 2/2 with no evasion whose first ability is a combat-damage trigger (verified stack 001 step 11: not an at-will repeatable placement, worth at most one extra iteration per combat), and ~120 combined life behind three defences kills incremental damage plans outright (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry). Role is seat-relative and re-asked every turn cycle (strategy:whos-the-beatdown, strategy:pivot-point): against a faster combo deck or an assembling lock you are forced into the racing seat and must tutor for a kill rather than for the grind (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial).
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: Pivot to an all-out win attempt when BOTH halves are live: a repeatable -1/-1 source (Yawgmoth, or Mikaeus + Devoted Druid) AND a converter that hits every seat (Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance or Obelisk Spider — Blood Artist drains one target player per death and is a value card, not a table clock). Goldfish sets the honest odds: any drain converter 51.9% overall, 41.5% by turn 6, mean turn 3.34; the source class is two cards deep and the verified Mikaeus + Devoted Druid pairing assembles 2.5% unassisted, 31.7% with a tutor, mean turn 5.69. That gap IS the pivot discipline — unassisted you are pacing for the median and taking the ceiling opportunistically; a tutor in hand is what converts the ceiling into a plan. Secondary trigger: Hapatra + Blowfly Infestation assembled (16.3% overall, 12.5% by turn 6, mean turn 4.10) — that line is queued for verification and may not be played as though it were settled. Fire when the table's interaction is counted and spent, not when the board looks impressive; at bracket 4 assume every held answer appears the moment you present the loop, and sequence the scariest piece last (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). Prefer the attempt that leaves a rebuilt position — Snakes, Bitterblossom and Blood Artist make a failed attempt cheap (strategy:resource-hedging).

engines.engine: The mint, not the source. Her second ability is the half that matters — every -1/-1 counter placement anywhere becomes a 1/1 deathtouch Snake, so she is the exchange rate between someone else's counter and a body. Her combat trigger is the weak half and is a bonus, never a plan. She is also the deck's most reliable card: cast on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs (mean 2.007, 99.9% by turn 6), and 'commander plus any -1/-1 payoff' assembles 67.2% of games at mean turn 3.62 off a six-card payoff class.
engines.evidence: oracle text (combat-damage trigger + 'Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create a 1/1 green Snake creature token with deathtouch'); verified stack 001 step 11 (checker verdict pass) classifies the first ability as combat-damage-only; goldfish_metrics commander block and target 1

engines.engine: The deck's only free repeatable -1/-1 source, and therefore the real tutor target. Stack 001's outlet census — re-derived by the adversarial checker from every 'sacrific' card in cards.json — finds eight mana-free sacrifice outlets (Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Yawgmoth, Blasting Station, Lazotep Quarry) and exactly one of them also PLACES a counter. That asymmetry is the whole deck: outlets are abundant, sources are two deep. Each activation costs 1 life, draws a card and needs a legal target on resolution — the single instance of 'target' means an illegal target fizzles the whole ability, so a second body is mandatory. With Mikaeus it loops for real and is library-bounded by its own mandatory draw: a strong engine, not a true infinite.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 steps 10 and 12 (checker verdict pass, 4 iterations); oracle text ('Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card'); combo_details lists Hapatra + Yawgmoth + Obelisk Spider and Hapatra + Yawgmoth + Blood Artist as contained bracket-3 lines

engines.engine: The deck's one verified true two-card infinite — of deaths, -1/-1 placements, Snakes and drain, explicitly NOT of mana. Steady state without haste is four counter placements and one death per cycle at zero mana, because the returned Druid is a new object that has not been under your control since your turn began (302.6 blocks its tap ability); the first pass yields three green and every pass after yields none. Lightning Greaves or Swiftfoot Boots restore the mana as a three-card, main-phase-only line (four green with Greaves, three with Boots), but Greaves' shroud then shuts Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting the Druid. Price it honestly: Mikaeus is a one-card component, which is 7.1% of an opening seven and 9.1% by turn 3, and the pairing measures 2.5% assembled / 1.3% by turn 6 unassisted, 31.7% / 19.8% with a tutor, mean turn 5.69. That is a ceiling, not a plan.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 steps 13-14 and 16 (checker verdict pass; the nine-step haste cycle and the zero-mana steady state were independently re-derived); goldfish target 'Mikaeus + Devoted Druid (the two-card infinite stack 001 verified)'; deck-audit engine block, thinnest component 1 card

engines.piece: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed + Walking Ballista + any free sacrifice outlet
engines.engine: The cleanest verified kill in the deck, and a three-card assembly rather than two. Mikaeus's +1/+1 is a layer-7c modification applied alongside counters, so a counterless Ballista is a 1/1 under Mikaeus and 704.5f never fires — the classic 'remove the last counter and it dies' pattern is switched off and an external free outlet is mandatory. Per iteration: 1 damage plus whatever the outlet yields. Genuinely unbounded, and it converts to a win with no drain payoff at all, which makes it the line to tutor toward when the converter class has already been answered.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 step 15 (613.4c, 704.5f, 702.93a; checker verdict pass)

engines.piece: The Mikaeus altar entries — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Blasting Station, Yahenni, Undying Partisan
engines.engine: A stated finding, not a loop: each of these yields exactly one undying return and stops. Undying only returns a creature that died with no +1/+1 counter on it, and nothing in that pairing strips the counter it comes back with; Hapatra cannot supply the reset, because her placement is a combat-damage trigger. A Snake token is worse still — it ceases to exist as a state-based action before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack, so undying returns nothing. Counter annihilation does reset undying, but only when the annihilation and the death fall in different state-based-action checks; 704.8 kills the trigger when they coincide. Practical consequence at the table: with Mikaeus out, sacrificing to a free altar is a value activation worth one extra death, and it should be sequenced as one.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 final_state and steps 1-12 (checker verdict pass, 4 iterations, override recorded in the artifact); deck-facts lists these six pairings among the 19 two-card infinites contained in the deck

engines.piece: Zulaport Cutthroat / Bastion of Remembrance / Obelisk Spider (and Blood Artist, one tier down)
engines.engine: The converter class — the only cards that turn any loop into a win, and the axis on which the multiplayer correction bites. Zulaport, Bastion and Obelisk Spider drain EACH opponent; Blood Artist's drain names one target player per death, so it is a value card and a wrath tax rather than a table clock. Obelisk Spider is the outlier: it drains on counter PLACEMENT, not on death, so against the Devoted Druid steady state of four placements and one death per cycle it converts four times faster than a death-trigger drain. This is the class strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry insists on — something that touches all three seats.
engines.evidence: oracle text (all four); verified stack 001 step 16 confirms Blood Artist converts the Druid loop at one life per cycle from a player of your choice; goldfish target 'Any drain converter' 51.9% assembled / 41.5% by turn 6, mean turn 3.34

engines.piece: Skullclamp + Grim Haruspex + Morbid Opportunist + Deadly Dispute + Village Rites + Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER
engines.engine: The bodies-to-cards layer that carries the median game when no loop exists, and the reason this list is an engine deck rather than a combo pile. Snakes are 1/1, so Skullclamp is two cards for {1} on every one of them; Grim Haruspex draws off every nontoken death; Deadly Dispute and Village Rites turn a spare body into two cards at instant speed. deck-audit counts eight card-advantage copies against a template floor of ten, but names three more the taxonomy files elsewhere — Grim Backwoods, The One Ring and Yawgmoth all draw cards, and Yawgmoth draws one per activation. Read that axis as a floor rather than a shortfall.
engines.evidence: oracle text; deck-audit card-advantage axis (value 8, target >= 10, possible_uncounted: Grim Backwoods, The One Ring, Yawgmoth, Thran Physician); synergy_graph lists Sephiroth as an in-deck Hapatra partner

engines.piece: Necroskitter + Black Sun's Zenith / Serrated Arrows / Contagion Clasp
engines.engine: The asymmetric-sweeper package. Black Sun's Zenith puts X -1/-1 counters on EACH creature, which is one placement event Hapatra sees and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it — one card as a wipe, a Snake wave and a mass reanimation at once. The sharp caveat is verified from oracle text: Toxic Deluge gives -X/-X until end of turn and places no counters, so it triggers neither Hapatra nor Necroskitter nor Nest of Scarabs. It is a pure reset button and should be sequenced as one.
engines.evidence: oracle text (Black Sun's Zenith 'Put X -1/-1 counters on each creature'; Toxic Deluge 'All creatures get -X/-X until end of turn'; Necroskitter; Serrated Arrows; Contagion Clasp); Necroskitter verified ABSENT from combo_graph partners

engines.piece: The eight-tutor package (Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Imperial Seal, Worldly Tutor, Survival of the Fittest, Green Sun's Zenith, Diabolic Intent, Grim Tutor)
engines.engine: The consistency purchase that makes a two-deep enabler class playable at all: k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of it, and strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors prices the alternative — '5 copies is 31% of openers, 7 is 41% ... 10 is 54%'. Goldfish has a tutor drawn in 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6, mean turn 2.70, and tutor assistance is what moves the Mikaeus + Devoted Druid line from 2.5% to 31.7%. The default target is a repeatable -1/-1 source, and failing that a converter that drains all three seats. Diabolic Intent and Survival of the Fittest cost a body or a card, which is nearly free in this shell; Green Sun's Zenith putting Devoted Druid or Ivy Lane Denizen straight onto the battlefield is the tempo line.
engines.evidence: deck-audit tutors axis (8 copies, target 4-8 under the combo archetype, verdict at) and its redundancy_citation; goldfish target 'Any tutor drawn' 0.780 / 0.676 by turn 6; verified stack 001 final_state names a free repeatable -1/-1 source as the tutor target that matters

candidate_missing_lines.title: The Blowfly family — Blowfly Infestation + Hapatra, + Nest of Scarabs, + Flourishing Defenses
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Three of the 19 two-card infinites deck-facts finds contained in this deck, and combo_details lists Hapatra, Nest of Scarabs and Flourishing Defenses as in-deck Blowfly partners. Oracle chain: Blowfly triggers whenever a creature dies if it had a -1/-1 counter on it, putting a -1/-1 counter on target creature; that placement triggers Hapatra (or Nest, or Defenses) to make a fresh 1/1 token; the 1/1 that received the counter becomes 0/0 and dies carrying a -1/-1 counter, re-triggering Blowfly. This is the line goldfish tracks at 16.3% assembled / 12.5% by turn 6 and the one the pilot is most likely to reach, and it is not settled. A scenario must decide whether the loop is optional enough to avoid a draw (Blowfly's placement is mandatory but the target is chosen, so the escape is targeting an opponent's creature — 104.4b / 732 territory, exactly the analysis stack 001 step 16 ran for the Druid loop), whether it needs a seed counter and a spare token to start, and what happens when no legal target remains.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Does Mikaeus's anthem switch the Blowfly and Hapatra token loops OFF?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Oracle text, unresolved, and it cuts against the deck's own plan. Mikaeus gives other non-Human creatures +1/+1. Snakes, Insects and Elf Warriors are all non-Human, so under Mikaeus they are 2/2, and a single -1/-1 counter leaves a 1/1 rather than reducing them to 0 toughness. If that reading holds, the token half of every Blowfly loop stops killing its own fodder and terminates, meaning the deck's two headline engines are mutually exclusive on the battlefield. Stack 001 step 15 established that Mikaeus's anthem changes exactly this kind of arithmetic for Walking Ballista via layer 7c, which is why the same question deserves its own resolution for the token loops. It is the highest-value open question in the deck and it changes sequencing, not just theory.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen, and the Ivy Lane + Devoted Druid three-card family
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details names Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen as the highest-bracket line contained in this deck (bracket 4, popularity 24,313) and stack 001 deliberately declined to rest the bracket floor on it. The pairing reads clean on oracle text — Ivy Lane puts a +1/+1 counter on target creature whenever another green creature you control enters; Scurry Oak may create a 1/1 green Squirrel whenever one or more +1/+1 counters are put on it; the Squirrel is a green creature entering — but the Squirrel step is a 'may', and the line produces no win without a converter, so a scenario must settle both the loop and its conversion. The sibling three-card entries (Ivy Lane + Devoted Druid + Hapatra / Nest of Scarabs / Flourishing Defenses, each listed as infinite green mana plus infinite tokens) turn on the Druid's untap and belong in the same scenario. Explicitly NOT queued: the six Ivy Lane pairings with a sacrifice outlet. On the named pair alone no green creature enters, so Ivy Lane never triggers and there is no loop without an unlisted third piece — the same projection shape stack 001 exposed on the Mikaeus half.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Yawgmoth + Hapatra without Mikaeus — the deck's most realistic actual kill
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details holds Hapatra + Yawgmoth + Obelisk Spider and Hapatra + Yawgmoth + Blood Artist as contained bracket-3 lines producing near-infinite lifeloss and 'destroy all creatures opponents control', and stack 001 verified Yawgmoth's mechanics only inside the Mikaeus line. Oracle chain without Mikaeus: sacrifice a Snake to Yawgmoth, place the -1/-1 counter on a creature that survives it (one of your larger bodies, or an opponent's creature), Hapatra sees the placement and mints a replacement Snake — net Snake count flat, one card drawn, one life paid, one death trigger per activation. That is a life-and-library-bounded engine that draws your deck and drains the table with any converter out, and it needs neither Mikaeus nor Blowfly. It is plausibly the line this deck wins with most often and it has never been resolved. The scenario must settle the target-survives requirement, the fizzle rule stack 001 step 12 identified (a single instance of 'target', so an illegal target means no draw at all), and the life and library bounds.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Yawgmoth + Scurry Oak + a drain converter as an infinite-draw line
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Three contained combo_details entries pair Yawgmoth and Scurry Oak with each of Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and Bastion of Remembrance, all tagged infinite card draw plus near-infinite death triggers. Oracle reading: Yawgmoth's activation places a -1/-1 counter and draws; the counter placement is not what Scurry Oak wants, so the loop must be running on the Squirrel bodies as sacrifice fodder and on evolve or another +1/+1 source to re-arm the Oak. That gap is exactly why it needs resolution — the pieces are all in the 99 and the produces list claims infinite draw, but the engine's re-arming step is not visible on the two named cards and Yawgmoth's draw is mandatory, so a genuine infinite here would deck you. Settle whether it loops, and if it does, where the safe exit is.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: A contained two-card infinite in combo_details and Host's only combo partner anywhere in the graph. Oracle chain: a Snake carrying a -1/-1 counter dies, Host moves its counters onto another creature you control, that placement triggers Hapatra to mint a fresh Snake, the recipient goes to 0 toughness and dies carrying the counter, Host triggers again. Elegant and plausible, and it turns on two things a scenario must decide: whether Host's counter-moving counts as 'putting' counters for Hapatra's trigger, and whether 'up to one target creature you control' gives a clean loop exit rather than a mandatory one.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Necroskitter + Black Sun's Zenith as a one-sided wipe-and-steal
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Not a combo_details entry — Necroskitter is verified absent from the partners map — so this is pure oracle reasoning and must not be presented as a play until it is resolved. Black Sun's Zenith puts X -1/-1 counters on each creature; opposing creatures that die with a counter on them should each give Necroskitter its optional return trigger, while Hapatra sees the placement. The interactions to settle are the state-based-action timing (do the deaths all happen in one check, and does Necroskitter's 'may return that card' see them from the graveyard), and how many Snake triggers Hapatra actually gets from a single mass placement, since her trigger reads 'one or more ... on a creature'. If it works it is the deck's single best card against a creature-heavy table.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: You are structurally well-placed and should still sequence carefully. Your board is mostly free tokens; Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep for 1 life, Skullclamp and Grim Haruspex convert the loss into cards, and Blood Artist triggers on ANY creature dying, so a table wrath with Blood Artist out is a large drain aimed wherever you like. That is 'buy resilience instead of restraint' already paid for at deckbuild time (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). The asymmetry runs the other way for your ceiling: Hapatra, Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Ivy Lane Denizen, Scurry Oak and Necroskitter are all creatures, so a wrath is nearly one-sided against your combo half while being cheap against your token half. Deploy in waves, lead with the token half, hold the combo half until the pivot window, and assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). Your own Black Sun's Zenith is a rebuild rather than a reset: it is the sweeper that feeds Hapatra, Nest of Scarabs and Necroskitter, while Toxic Deluge feeds none of them.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: The worst matchup, and the one the binding axis names. deck-audit puts interaction-breadth at 1 class of 5 against a target of 5, with artifact, enchantment, graveyard and land all showing zero — the 14 interactive copies inside a 20-card interactive suite all answer creatures. Read the cards before calling a class dead, as the audit itself insists: Abstergo Entertainment's {3}, {T}, exile-itself ability does exile all graveyards, and Talon Gates of Madara phases out a creature. That still leaves no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell and no land answer, which is precisely the failure strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite warns about — 'Stax is the hardest breadth test'. So role assignment is forced: you do not own the long game under an assembling lock, and you are the beatdown racing its completion (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial, strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Your outs are speed, politics and someone else's removal — name them on turn one and sequence to protect them (strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs). Two things genuinely favour you: the kill is cheap, and your commander lands on turn 2 in 99.7% of goldfish runs, so you can often be under the lock before its second and third pieces layer.
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: Your best matchup, for a reason that never shows up in a removal count. A 1/1 deathtouch Snake is virtual interaction: it blanks any attacker regardless of size, so a board of Snakes turns an opposing creature deck's best cards into cards they cannot profitably use (strategy:card-advantage.virtual — a card that blanks several opposing cards generates advantage without drawing anything, and in Commander that triples across three seats). Behind that, Black Sun's Zenith and Toxic Deluge are catch-up buttons and Necroskitter converts their aggression into your board. Life is spendable here and this deck spends it constantly — Yawgmoth activations, Phyrexian Reclamation, The One Ring's burden counters, Bitterblossom, Toxic Deluge's additional cost, three painlands — so track which single opponent's clock is real and defend against that one rather than the table (strategy:life-as-resource, strategy:multiplayer.pod-management). Do not convert a good matchup into a bad seat by attacking with Hapatra into open blockers for one marginal counter trigger.
matchup_frames.vs_combo: Symmetrically thin, and you should play it as a race rather than an interaction game. You hold no counterspell and no answer to an artifact or enchantment, so the only combo decks you can touch are creature-based ones — and there you do have instant-speed answers worth holding (Grim Affliction, Fume Spitter's free sacrifice, Walking Ballista's ping, Serrated Arrows). The answer-economy rule inverts here: held answers rot, and against combo the last profitable moment is now (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Rank combo proximity above every board threat and re-rank every turn (strategy:threat-assessment). Your own race is real but slow — Hapatra + Blowfly assembles 16.3% overall, 12.5% by turn 6 at mean turn 4.10 and is not yet verified, and the verified Mikaeus + Devoted Druid line is 2.5% unassisted at mean turn 5.69. Do not plan to out-speed a dedicated combo deck on raw assembly; plan to be the deck the table's interaction is not pointed at, deploy Snakes that read as defensive, and take your window while three players watch each other (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). One caution specific to this list: the 11 Game Changers are the tell. The moment a Mox, a Demonic Tutor or The One Ring hits the table, the deflection budget the Snakes bought you is spent.
matchup_frames.vs_creature_midrange: The default pod seat and the one the deck is actually built for. You out-grind fair creature decks on two axes at once: their removal is bad against tokens, and their attacks are bad into deathtouch. Hold single-target removal until a threat is pointed at you rather than spending it on sight — every one-for-one you cast in a four-player game is a net gift to two bystanders (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry, strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Win by out-carding them through the Snake-to-cards layer, then pivot the moment a table-wide drain converter joins a repeatable counter source (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).

distribution_notes: Read from deck-facts, deck-audit, mana_analysis and goldfish_metrics. Shape: 88 entries / 100 copies, 36 land copies across 24 land entries, 64 nonland entries, curve 4 zero-drops / 16 one / 19 two / 17 three / 6 four / 1 five / 1 six and a modal mana value of 2 — squarely the shape strategy:deckbuilding.curve describes, and goldfish confirms it plays out (mean available mana 2.46 on turn 2, 4.71 on turn 4, 6.15 on turn 6, so Mikaeus at six is a real turn-6 card and everything else is castable ahead of schedule). Mana is the strongest part of the list and is over-built rather than under: 36 lands sits inside the 36-38 template band, zero lands enter tapped, no mana in the deck is restricted in a way that cannot pay an activated ability, and colour sources run 37 black and 39 green against a Karsten 90% target of 22 each — 15 above target on the worst colour. Counting persistent producers, mana-sources is 50 against a Burgess target of 35 (31 + 2 colours + commander mana value 2). Consistency follows: keep-first-seven 79.9%, mean mulligans 0.243, turn-3 land drop 90.2%, commander cast on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs. Two axes sit off template. Ramp is 16 copies against 10-12 — four over, which is the deliberate price of a turn-2 commander and three zero-cost rocks, and it is why land-drop hit rate slides to 64.9% by turn 5 without hurting the plan. Card advantage counts 8 against a floor of 10, but deck-audit names three more the taxonomy files elsewhere (Grim Backwoods, The One Ring, and Yawgmoth, whose sacrifice ability draws a card per activation), so that axis is a floor rather than a hole. The binding axis is neither: interaction-breadth is 1 class of 5 against a target of 5, with artifact, enchantment, graveyard and land uncovered. The count is fine — 14 interactive copies inside a 20-card interactive suite clears Walser's 8-10 removal baseline — and the breadth is not, which is exactly the ordering strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite puts on it. Everything else reads at target: 2 sweepers, 5 protection, 6 finishers on Zupke's floor of at least three, 25 creatures, 8 tutors inside the combo band of 4-8, bracket floor 4 on 11 Game Changers. Engine redundancy is where the shape gets uncomfortable and the numbers are unambiguous. The payoff class is six deep (Nest of Scarabs, Flourishing Defenses, Obelisk Spider, Blood Artist, Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance) and assembles alongside the commander 67.2% of the time at mean turn 3.62; the drain-converter class is four deep at 51.9%; a tutor is drawn in 78.0% of games. Against that, both combo targets rest on a single named card — Blowfly Infestation and Mikaeus each 7.1% of an opening seven, 9.1% by turn 3 — and the verified Mikaeus + Devoted Druid pairing measures 2.5% assembled, 1.3% by turn 6, mean turn 5.69, rising to 31.7% once a tutor is counted. deck-facts finds 32 combo lines fully contained here and 19 two-card infinites; six of those 19 are refuted outright by verified stack 001, one is verified as a true infinite of deaths rather than mana, one is real but three cards, and eleven are unresolved. Redundancy is genuine in the median layer and one card deep at the ceiling — the exact asymmetry strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors prices when it puts a 7-of at 41% of openers, and the reason eight tutors are not excessive here.
overall_assessment: This deck is playing a converter's game, and the most useful thing anyone can tell its pilot is that Hapatra is not an engine — she is a mint. She does not generate -1/-1 counters at will (verified stack 001 step 11: that half of her is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2); she monetises counters other cards place, one deathtouch body each. That inverts the usual reading of the list. The scarce half is the counter SOURCE — not the outlet, not the payoff. Stack 001's census found eight mana-free sacrifice outlets in the 99 and exactly one that also places a counter, Yawgmoth, plus Devoted Druid under Mikaeus. Everything downstream is abundant: Snakes, Insects, Elf Warriors, Skullclamp draws, Blood Artist drains, Necroskitter steals. So the tutor target is a source, and the mulligan test is 'does this hand contain a route to a repeatable source', not 'does it contain a payoff' — strategy:mulligans.engine-hands is blunt that payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists, and that in 100-card singleton you mulligan to enabler CLASSES rather than named cards. The second thing to tell the pilot is that the combo ceiling is narrower than a combo count suggests, and the deck's own artifacts now say so. Of the 19 two-card infinites deck-facts finds contained here, six are refuted by four resolver passes under four adversarial checks: Mikaeus paired with Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Blasting Station or Yahenni each yields exactly one undying return, because a token ceases to exist before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack and a non-token creature returns carrying a +1/+1 counter that nothing in the pairing strips. What survives is Mikaeus + Devoted Druid as a true two-card infinite of deaths, counters, Snakes and drain but explicitly NOT of mana; Mikaeus + Walking Ballista as a real kill that needs a third card; and Yawgmoth, which loops for real and is library-bounded by its own mandatory draw. The remaining eleven — three Blowfly entries, six Ivy Lane pairings, Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen and Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter — are unresolved, and none may be spoken of as fact. Goldfish now prices the survivor honestly: 2.5% assembled, 1.3% by turn 6, mean turn 5.69, and 31.7% once a tutor is counted. That is a ceiling to take opportunistically, not a plan to pace for, which is precisely the discipline strategy:critical-mass.storm-math and strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density both demand — separate ceiling from median, pace for the median, hold the ceiling as opportunism. The median is strong: a turn-2 commander in 99.7% of runs, a payoff beside her 67.2% of the time by mean turn 3.6, a drain converter 51.9%, and a Snake-to-cards layer deep enough to out-draw three players (strategy:card-advantage). Play it from the control seat, own inevitability once a repeatable source meets a table-wide converter (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock), keep the perceived threat level under the actual one for as long as 11 Game Changers let you (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection), and take one counted pivot window rather than the first loop that looks like it works (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). The build's real departure is not its interaction COUNT — 14 interactive copies inside a 20-card suite clears Walser's baseline — it is that all of it points at creatures, leaving interaction-breadth at 1 class of 5. strategy:critical-mass licenses part of that ('interaction slots are the price of the engine', and the linear deck's defence is 'speed, redundancy, and resilience, not answers'), and this deck delivers speed and resilience in abundance. It does not deliver breadth, and strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite is explicit that breadth comes before depth because three opponents mean every permanent type appears. So the correct price on the departure is not one card below a template count; it is that the deck has no line against permanent-based prison or an artifact/enchantment combo, and pays for that with a matchup family it must race or politick rather than answer. Against a creature-heavy pod that is a legitimate bracket-4 trade; against a prison pod it is a losing one — which makes it a Rule 0 conversation rather than a build error.
gaps: No section on auditing a combo list. The difference between a graph-listed two-card infinite and a line that works in YOUR 99 is the single most load-bearing idea in this deck's frame, and the doc has nothing on it. Wanted: how to price an unverified combo count, why pairwise combo data silently drops third pieces and assumes commanders, and what a deck's verified-kill count should do to its self-image and its bracket conversation.

No aristocrats / sacrifice-engine section. The outlet / fodder / converter taxonomy, the distinction between free and mana-costed outlets, why a free repeatable outlet is a different card class from a costed one, and the drain-converter tiering (each-opponent versus single-target) all had to be derived here from oracle text. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math is the nearest neighbour and it is about spell velocity, not body velocity.

No counters-matter section. -1/-1 counters as removal that pays you, counter annihilation as a resource, the anthem-versus-shrink anti-synergy (an anthem that makes your own fodder too big to die to your own removal), and the difference between counter-based and stat-modifying mass removal (Black Sun's Zenith versus Toxic Deluge) are all real strategic content with no home in the doc.

No tutor-sequencing section for pilots. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors covers the deckbuilding count well but says nothing about the in-game decision: with eight tutors and a two-deep enabler class, WHAT you fetch and WHEN — source before converter, converter before protection — is a distinct skill, and so is how a refuted primary target should rewrite the default.

No fast-mana section. Mana Vault, Grim Monolith, Chrome Mox, Mox Diamond, Lotus Petal and Dark Ritual each trade a real resource (a card, an untap step, life, a land) for speed, and the doc has no framework for when that trade is correct versus when it is the reason you lose to the first piece of interaction. This deck is four ramp copies over template and the doc cannot say whether that is a defect or the point.

No section on engine redundancy asymmetry — a deck whose median layer is six deep and whose ceiling rests on one named card at 7.1% of an opening seven. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors prices copies and tutors; strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density prices finishers; neither addresses what to do when those two numbers disagree by an order of magnitude inside one list.
